subject: Biology
title: The Tree of Life
description: A 60-second lesson on The Tree of Life.

hook.text: Every living thing on Earth—from bacteria to blue whales—shares a single common ancestor.

buildup.text: The tree of life maps evolutionary relationships between all species, living and extinct.

discovery.text: DNA comparison reveals that humans share 60% of genes with bananas and 98.7% with chimpanzees.

twist.text: Horizontal gene transfer between bacteria means the 'tree' is actually more like a tangled web at its base.

climax.text: Metagenomics is revealing millions of previously unknown microbial species, expanding the tree enormously.

punchline.text: One root. Billions of branches. All connected.

quiz.question: What percentage of genes do humans share with chimpanzees?

details.summary: The tree of life is a metaphor and model mapping evolutionary relationships among all living organisms. Its three main branches, Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya, diverged billions of years ago, and molecular phylogenetics continues to refine our understanding of how species are related.
details.whyItMatters: The tree of life reveals that all organisms share common ancestry, connecting humans to bacteria through an unbroken chain of descent. It organizes biological diversity and predicts evolutionary relationships even for newly discovered species.
takeaways: All life belongs to three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya
Molecular data has revolutionized our understanding of evolutionary relationships
Horizontal gene transfer makes parts of the tree resemble a tangled web

faq.question: How do scientists build the tree of life?
faq.answer: By comparing DNA, RNA, or protein sequences across species. Shared similarities indicate closer relationships. Computational algorithms analyze millions of base pairs to find the tree that best explains observed patterns. Fossils calibrate the timing of branch points.

faq.question: Is the tree of life actually tree-shaped?
faq.answer: Not entirely. Horizontal gene transfer, hybridization, and endosymbiosis create reticulate connections between branches. Among bacteria, the tree resembles a web more than a tree. For eukaryotes, the branching tree pattern holds better, though some cross-connections exist.
